2024_203_boe_2_6_24_course_description_b.paragraph: High school Course Description Book updates were presented to the Troy School District Board of Education on February 6, 2024, covering alignment of Computer Science, renaming of Business courses, and a slate of new offerings: AP Art History, Chemistry 1 and Chemistry 2, Physics 1 and Physics 2, Engineering Physics, Environmental Science: Human Impact, English 10, Stories of Yourself & Others, Digital Business, and Business Law & Management. Presenters reported that approximately 94% of students from the ungrouped ELA 9 pilot who matriculated to 10 LC Honors earned an A or B in the first quarter. Graduation requirements also change: Personal Finance becomes a 0.5-credit requirement for the class of 2028, with its standards embedded in Economics and AP Economics.
2024_203_boe_2_6_24_course_description_b.page:
**Presentation:** HS Course Description Book Updates, Troy School District Board of Education, February 6, 2024.

**Course updates (existing offerings)**
- Alignment of Computer Science
- Renaming of Business courses: Marketing 2; Marketing Field Study Co-Op; Junior Business Field Study Co-Op; Senior Business Field Study Co-Op

**New courses proposed**
| Area | Courses |
|---|---|
| Art/History | AP Art History |
| Science | Chemistry 1 & Chemistry 2; Physics 1 & Physics 2; Engineering Physics; Environmental Science: Human Impact |
| English | English 10 |
| Social Studies | Stories of Yourself & Others |
| Business | Digital Business; Business Law & Management |

**Selected course specifications**
- AP Art History: Grades 11-12, 2 semesters, 1/2 credit per semester, no retake; prerequisite World History/Geography 1 and American History/Geography 1 & 2. Built on 250 works of art from prehistory to the present; equivalent to a two-semester introductory college art history survey.
- Stories of Yourself & Others: Grade 12, 1 semester, 1/2 ELA credit and 1/2 History credit, no retake; same prerequisites. Interdisciplinary, inquiry-based course on storytelling and narrative through the lens of Reconstruction history, using Socratic Seminar discussion and a culminating student research project.
- Digital Business: Grades 9-12, 1 semester, 1/2 credit, no retake, no prerequisite. Uses Microsoft Office (Word, Excel, PowerPoint), Wordpress, Canva, and responsible/ethical use of AI systems, with the goal of Microsoft Office Specialist certification.
- Business Law & Management: Grades 9-12, 1 semester, 1/2 credit, no retake, no prerequisite. Covers global trade, quality management, organizational structure, human resource law, workplace ethics, torts, negligence, contracts, fraud, and legal requirements for starting a business.
- English 10: 2 semesters, 1 credit, 1/2 credit per semester; required for all 10th grade students. Builds on English 9; multimodal texts, analytical lenses, real-world writing, book clubs, independent reading plan; summer reading required.

**Science**
New State of Michigan graduation requirements drove new course development, affecting the class of 2027 (this year's freshmen) and beyond. Board of Education visits were made to Athens High School and Troy High School. All graduation-required courses are designed for all students around NGSS standards, shifting toward "students figuring out science" with emphasis on inquiry and design.

**ELA pilot results (first quarter of 10 Honors)**
| School | Moved from ELA 9 pilot to 10 Honors | A | B | C or lower |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Troy High | 154 of 190 | 117 (76%) | 28 (18%) | 9 (6%) |
| Athens HS | 67 of 87 | 42 (63%) | 20 (30%) | 5 (7%) |

Approximately 94% of pilot participants who matriculated to 10 LC Honors earned an A or B in Q1.

**CommonLit assessment (grades 6-12 outcome measure)**
Each assessment has three reading passages with multiple-choice comprehension questions.

| Group | Submitted count | Pre-assessment (September) | Mid-year (December/January) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10th grade nationally | 98101 | 196 | 202 |
| 10th grade across TSD | 847 | 200 | 206 |
| 10th grade Honors in pilot | 187 | 206 | 215 |

**Graduation requirements**
Personal Finance is added for the class of 2028, granting 0.5 credit and indicated as a graduation requirement on the transcript; standards will be embedded in Economics and AP Economics, which students do not enroll in until grade 11. Flexibility exists at TCCHS, Athens High School and Troy High School, including math-related fourth-year options and CTE.

**Support and next steps**
Three ELA 10 units are developed with three more planned for spring, summer revision work, and all students enrolled in ELA 10 for 2024-25. Supports include job-embedded learning days, three planning days for the English 10 curriculum development team, on-site staff developer visits, the Homegrown Institute, and continued coaching positions at both high schools. Future data review will use PSAT 9 (released this summer), PSAT 10, SAT 11, AP Lit and AP Language enrollment and outcomes, and student, teacher and parent surveys.
2024_203_boe_2_6_24_course_description_b.verbose:
HS Course Description Book Updates, presented to the Troy School District Board of Education at its February 6, 2024 meeting, sets out proposed changes to the high school course catalog across Computer Science, Business, Science, English Language Arts, Social Studies and Art, together with changes to graduation requirements.

OVERVIEW OF COURSE UPDATES
The overview section lists alignment of Computer Science and the renaming of Business courses, specifically Marketing 2, Marketing Field Study Co-Op, Junior Business Field Study Co-Op, and Senior Business Field Study Co-Op.

NEW COURSES
The new courses are grouped by department: Art/History - AP Art History; Science - Chemistry 1 & Chemistry 2, Physics 1 & Physics 2, Engineering Physics, and Environmental Science: Human Impact; English - English 10; Social Studies - Stories of Yourself & Others; Business - Digital Business and Business Law & Management.

AP Art History is offered in grades 11-12 over 2 semesters for 1/2 credit per semester with no retake, and carries the prerequisite of World History/Geography 1 and American History/Geography 1 & 2. The course description states that it welcomes students into the global art world to engage with its forms and content as they research, discuss, read and write about art, artists, art making, and responses to and interpretations of art. Students investigate 250 works of art characterized by diverse artistic traditions from prehistory to the present, developing in-depth, holistic understanding of the history of art from a global perspective, and apply skills of visual, contextual and comparative analysis. The course is described as the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college or university art history survey course.

Stories of Yourself & Others is a grade 12, one-semester course granting 1/2 ELA credit and 1/2 History credit, with no retake and the prerequisite of World History/Geography 1 and American History/Geography 1 & 2. It is an interdisciplinary, inquiry-based course exploring the power of storytelling, writing and narrative through the lens of Reconstruction history. Students investigate the role of identity in marginalized communities during the Reconstruction Era by evaluating and synthesizing primary and secondary resources; fiction and non-fiction narratives modeling self-reflection and storytelling are read and discussed in a Socratic Seminar format. The course culminates in a student research project into the student's own history and identity or a self-selected marginalized group, presented in a medium of the student's choice.

Digital Business is open to grades 9-12, runs one semester for 1/2 credit, has no retake and no prerequisite. Students work with hands-on business applications using Microsoft Office, blogging and website-building platforms such as Wordpress, online graphic design programs such as Canva, and the responsible and ethical use of AI systems. Coverage includes Word, Excel and PowerPoint, with the goal that students become certified through the Microsoft Office Specialist Program. Students use the three applications to create documents, presentations and spreadsheets in a "mock" business setting. Resumes, cover letters, interview skills, presentation skills and career search skills are discussed, along with introductory business topics such as data analysis for business decisions, planning tools to guide organizational and departmental activities, and developing policies and procedures to protect workplace security.

Business Law & Management is open to grades 9-12, runs one semester for 1/2 credit, with no retake and no prerequisite. Over a semester students study law and management topics relating to the business industry. Management content covers the impacts of global trade, managing internal and external business relationships to foster positive interactions, the nature and scope of quality management practices within a business, and designing organizational structure to facilitate business activities. Legal content covers current human resource laws and regulations, ethical behaviors in the workplace, torts, negligence, contracts and fraud, and legal requirements for starting a business.

SCIENCE UPDATES
The high school science course update section notes that new graduation requirements from the State of Michigan resulted in the development of new courses, and that this affects the class of 2027 and beyond - identified in the presentation as this year's freshmen. The section references Board of Education visits to Athens High School (AHS) and Troy High School (THS). All graduation-required courses are designed for all students around the NGSS standards, with a shift toward "students figuring out science" and an emphasis on inquiry and design. A slide titled HS Science Pathways accompanies the section.

ENGLISH LANGUAGE ARTS UPDATES
The ELA process review lists Class of 2027 ninth grade parent presentations in Spring 2023, publication of the pathway on the district website in March 2023, Board of Education visits in October 2023, teacher reflections, and input from ELA department heads, ELA coaches, ninth grade ELA teachers, tenth grade LC/LCH teachers and 11 AP teachers.

English 10 spans 2 semesters for 1 credit, at 1/2 credit per semester, and is required for all 10th grade students. Completion of both the ninth and tenth grade foundational English courses is intended to prepare students to engage with future English courses, including Advanced Placement courses. The course builds on foundational skills established in English 9, expands critical thinking using multimodal texts and analytical lenses, and engages students in real-world writing tasks to develop voice and argumentation with consideration for purpose and audience. In addition to whole-class selections and book clubs, students select reading goals to develop an independent reading plan. Summer reading is required.

REPORT CARD DATA FROM THE ELA 9 PILOT
Student grades in 10 Honors for students coming from the English 9 pilot were reported for the first quarter. At Troy High, 154 of 190 students who moved from the English 9 pilot to 10 Honors earned: A, 117 students (76%); B, 28 students (18%); C or lower, 9 students (6%). At Athens High School, 67 of 87 students who moved from the English 9 pilot to 10 Honors earned: A, 42 students (63%); B, 20 students (30%); C or lower, 5 students (7%). The presentation states that approximately 94% of students who participated in the ELA 9 ungrouped pilot and matriculated to 10 LC Honors earned an A or B for Q1.

COMMONLIT ASSESSMENT
CommonLit is presented as the measure of outcomes for students in grades 6-12. Each CommonLit Assessment is composed of three reading passages, each accompanied by a set of multiple-choice comprehension questions measuring reading comprehension. CommonLit is described as a data tool used to identify whether students are progressing in the attainment of grade level standards, to inform classroom instruction, and to create and measure goal setting for students. The reported figures cover submitted count, the pre-assessment scaled score in September, and the mid-year assessment scaled score in December/January. Tenth grade nationally across CommonLit: submitted count 98101, pre-assessment 196, mid-year 202. Tenth grade across TSD: submitted count 847, pre-assessment 200, mid-year 206. Tenth grade Honors currently in the pilot: submitted count 187, pre-assessment 206, mid-year 215.

DATA REVIEW GOING FORWARD
Additional measures identified include PSAT 9 data, to be reviewed this summer when released; continued monitoring of PSAT 10 and SAT 11 data as curriculum is built for tenth and eleventh grade; monitoring of AP Lit and AP Language enrollment and outcome scores as students progress into eleventh and twelfth grade; and student, teacher and parent surveys.

TEACHER REFLECTIONS AND IMPLEMENTATION PLAN
Staff met with teachers in grades 9, 10 and 11 AP to reflect on current implementation of ELA 9 and to plan implementation of ELA 10, with successes and challenges informing next steps. For ELA 10 development and implementation, the curriculum team has developed three comprehensive units, three additional units will be developed in the spring, summer work will include opportunities for revision, and all students will be enrolled in ELA 10 for the 2024-25 school year.

The plan of support includes, for spring: two days of job-embedded work for ELA grade 9, three planning days for the English 10 Curriculum Development Team, on-site visits with a staff developer, grade 9 lab learning, and grade 10 support for the writing process for units. Summer support includes the Homegrown Institute and unit unpacking. Next year includes continued job-embedded learning for ninth and tenth grade, continued support of coaching positions at both high schools, and continued partnership with staff developers.

GRADUATION REQUIREMENTS
Changes include the inclusion of Personal Finance for the class of 2028. Personal Finance standards will be embedded into Economics and AP Economics. Personal Finance must be indicated as a graduation requirement and grant 0.5 credit on a student's transcript, effective for the class of 2028; students do not enroll in economics until grade 11. On flexibility, the presentation cites high levels of flexibility at TCCHS, flexibility at AHS and THS, opportunities for a math-related fourth year, CTE, and the Personal Finance 0.5 credit, which can count in lieu of a variety of graduation requirements for the class of 2028, along with a commitment to continued learning and collaboration in making recommendations.

RESOURCES FOR FAMILIES
The presentation directs families to the Teaching and Learning website and notes an upcoming parent night for future tenth grade parents.

2024_204_4_a_2024_2025_soc_recommendatio.paragraph: Recommendations for Schools of Choice for the 2024-2025 school year, presented by Deputy Superintendent Rick West to the Troy School District Board of Education on February 6, 2024, propose using Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projections as the basis for admissions and accepting applications for 11 kindergarten, 1 first grade and 7 middle school students, with middle school students placed by available space. Schools of Choice enrollment stood at 188 elementary students against 4,897 non-SOC students, or 3.70% district-wide at the elementary level, with Hill Elementary the highest at 17.14%. Additional students could be admitted in the third week of August if space allows.

2024_204_4_a_2024_2025_soc_recommendatio.verbose:
Item 4.a., Recommendations for Schools of Choice for the 2024-2025 School Year, was presented by Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, to the Troy School District Board of Education for the February 6, 2024 meeting. The packet includes a memorandum dated Tuesday, February 27, 2024, addressed to the TSD Board of Education from Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, on the subject of Schools of Choice Recommendations for the 2024-2025 School Year.

PROGRAM DESCRIPTION
Schools of Choice provides non-resident students with additional enrollment opportunities. Participation in Schools of Choice is optional for districts, and the degree and extent of participation are determined at the local level, including application enrollment dates, grade levels and building assignment.

ELEMENTARY ENROLLMENT PROJECTIONS SUBMITTED BY PLANTE MORAN CRESA
Projections and actuals for kindergarten and first grade are reported by school year. For 2021/2022, the kindergarten "Most Likely" projection was 845 (765 Kdg / 80 PreK) against an actual of 803 (723 Kdg / 80 PreK) as of 1/27/22, and the first grade "Most Likely" projection was 851 against an actual of 792 as of 1/27/22. For 2022/2023, the kindergarten "Most Likely" projection was 807 (737 Kdg / 70 PreK) against an actual of 881 (811 Kdg / 70 PreK) as of 1/27/23, with first grade "Most Likely" of 820 and actual of 762 as of 1/27/23. For 2023/2024, the kindergarten "Most Likely" projection was 777 (includes PreK) against an actual of 817 (727 Kdg / 90 PreK) as of 1/25/24, with first grade "Most Likely" of 821 and actual of 843 as of 1/25/24. For 2024/2025, the kindergarten "Most Likely" projection is 809 (732 Kdg / 77 PreK) and the first grade "Most Likely" projection is 729; actuals are shown as unknown.

SCHOOLS OF CHOICE STUDENTS BY ELEMENTARY BUILDING, 2023-2024
The data summary comparing elementary SOC and non-SOC students for the 2023-2024 school year reports, by building, the SOC count, non-SOC count, percentage SOC, and percentage change: Barnard Elementary 10 SOC and 416 non-SOC, 2.35%, change -1.62%; Bemis Elementary 1 and 454, 0.22%, change 0.01%; Costello Elementary 18 and 388, 4.43%, change -0.47%; Hamilton Elementary 13 and 440, 2.87%, change -0.50%; Hill Elementary 60 and 290, 17.14%, change 0.57%; Leonard Elementary 12 and 399, 2.92%, change -0.80%; Martell Elementary 7 and 366, 1.88%, change -0.71%; Morse Elementary 2 and 417, 0.48%, change -0.96%; Schroeder Elementary 0 and 450, 0.00%, change 0.00%; Troy Union Elementary 9 and 394, 2.23%, change -0.45%; TSD Preschool 0 and 90, 0.00%, change 0.00%; VLAC 0 and 6, 0.00%, change 0.00%; Wass Elementary 34 and 399, 7.85%, change -0.21%; and Wattles Elementary 22 and 388, 5.37%, change -1.09%.

SUBGROUP DATA
By subgroup, English Learner students number 27 among SOC students (14.36% of SOC, change -4.07%) and 1,321 among non-SOC students (26.98% of non-SOC, change -0.91%). Free/Reduced Lunch students number 48 among SOC (25.53%, change 0.65%) and 803 among non-SOC (16.40%, change 2.52%). Special Education students number 24 among SOC (12.77%, change 2.17%) and 564 among non-SOC (11.52%, change 1.84%).

GRADE-LEVEL DATA
By grade for 2023-2024: TSD preK, 0 SOC and 90 non-SOC, 0.00%, change 0.00%; Kindergarten, 15 SOC and 712 non-SOC, 2.06%, change -0.65%; First, 22 SOC and 821 non-SOC, 2.61%, change -2.64%; Second, 38 SOC and 757 non-SOC, 4.78%, change -0.45%; Third, 39 SOC and 809 non-SOC, 4.60%, change 0.35%; Fourth, 34 SOC and 825 non-SOC, 3.96%, change -0.61%; Fifth, 40 SOC and 883 non-SOC, 4.33%, change 0.54%. The elementary total is 188 SOC and 4,897 non-SOC, 3.70%, change -0.53%.

ETHNICITY DATA
By ethnicity among SOC students and non-SOC students respectively: Asian, 30 SOC (15.96%, change -2.01%) and 1,965 non-SOC (40.13%, change 0.13%); Black, 18 SOC (9.57%, change 1.28%) and 257 non-SOC (5.25%, change 0.41%); Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, 0 SOC (0.00%, change 0.00%) and 2 non-SOC (0.04%, change -0.02%); Hispanic, 10 SOC (5.32%, change 1.17%) and 304 non-SOC (6.21%, change 0.42%); Multi-ethnic, 14 SOC (7.45%, change 0.53%) and 260 non-SOC (5.31%, change 0.09%); Native American, 0 SOC (0.00%, change 0.00%) and 2 non-SOC (0.04%, change -0.04%); White, 116 SOC (61.70%, change -0.97%) and 2,107 non-SOC (43.03%, change -0.98%). Totals are 188 SOC (100%) and 4,897 non-SOC (100%), with change shown as NA.

NON-SCHOOLS OF CHOICE ENROLLMENT BY GRADE, 2023-2024
Non-SOC students by grade are reported as kindergarten 802*, first 821, second 757, third 809, fourth 825, fifth 883, sixth 948, seventh 918, eighth 885, ninth 869, tenth 956, eleventh 985 and twelfth 1008, for a total of 11,466. The asterisk indicates that the kindergarten total includes TSD PreK (Dev Kdg).

KINDERGARTEN AND FIRST GRADE HISTORY
A fifteen-year history of kindergarten and first grade enrollment is provided: 2009-2010, 739 and 817; 2010-2011, 752 and 785; 2011-2012, 727 and 832; 2012-2013, 768 and 795; 2013-2014, 766 and 814; 2014-2015, 700 and 787; 2015-2016, 755 and 728; 2016-2017, 798 and 769; 2017-2018, 812 and 845; 2018-2019, 800 and 871; 2019-2020, 792 and 845; 2020-2021, 734* and 785; 2021-2022, 764* and 744; 2022-2023, 859* and 722; and 2023-2024, 802* and 821. Asterisked kindergarten totals include TSD PreK (Dev Kdg).

SIBLING PREFERENCE PROJECTION
A survey was emailed to current Schools of Choice families requesting information on siblings who would be eligible for kindergarten, first grade, and sixth, seventh and eighth grade for the 2024-2025 school year. The results: 11 kindergarten students plan to attend, 1 first grade student plans to attend, and 7 middle school students plan to attend across sixth, seventh and eighth grades (2 in sixth grade, 4 in seventh grade, 1 in eighth grade).

MEMORANDUM AND RECOMMENDATIONS
The memorandum reproduces prior-year language describing factors considered for the 2016-2017 school year, which included current enrollment; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; projected numbers of Schools of Choice siblings age-eligible to enter the district in 2016-2017 if a "Limited" number of kindergarten, first and sixth through eighth grade students at Baker Middle School were admitted; and available elementary classrooms. That earlier recommendation was to use Fred Ignatovich's 1.5 enrollment projection numbers with his recommended formula (most likely + low/2) as the foundation; to accept SOC applications for 100 kindergarten and 30 first grade students, admitting 100 kindergartners initially with the option of admitting additional students in the third week of August if space allowed; to limit SOC kindergarten applicants to the full-day kindergarten program; and to accept "Sibling Preference" applications only for siblings of current SOC students, to attend Baker Middle School only, where estimated enrollment for the following year approximated 728 and accepting 15 applications during the initial application process would bring the district extremely close to an ideal total student population at Baker. It also noted that actual enrollment as of the February Count for both kindergarten and first grade was above both Mr. Ignatovich's "Most Likely" and "Low" 2015-16 projections, referenced in "Document 1."

For the 2024-2025 school year, the factors considered were current enrollment across the Troy School District; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; projected numbers of Schools of Choice siblings age-eligible to enter the district in 2024-2025 if a "Limited" number of kindergarten, first and sixth through eighth grade students were admitted under Schools of Choice; and available elementary classrooms.

After analyzing the data and factors, the recommendation is that the district use Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projection numbers as the foundation for determining the number of Schools of Choice students to admit for the 2024-2025 school year, and accept SOC applications for 11 kindergarten, 1 first grade and 7 middle school students. The memorandum states that based on the number of kindergarten applications received for the 2024-2025 school year, the district anticipates attracting many more than 11 applicants; this approach would allow the district to admit 11 kindergarteners initially, with the option of admitting additional students in the third week of August if space allows. Middle school students would be placed in a building according to available space.
